gallery.filename: D. Stacey to Thomas Field Letter In regards to Bull Run, 1861 (6789167997).jpg
gallery.title: File:D. Stacey to Thomas Field Letter In regards to Bull Run, 1861 (6789167997).jpg
gallery.description:
"Thomas you are hunting - I fully expected you here last Saturday, but was disappointed and to console myself took a trip to "Camp Downing" to see the soldiers. They are a fine body of men but look green, undisciplined and dirty. Bull's Run (or Yankee's Run as they call it here) was a most disgraceful affair. A friend of mine just arrived fought through it with the N.Y. 71st. He says they were outnumbered from the commencement of the fight, but if old Miles had brought up the reserve they would have been in Richmond in two days after. I don't believe it. It will take harder fighting and a great many more lives before we attain that point."
From the Charles L. McCawley Collection (COLL/2896) at the Marine Corps Archives and Special Collections

gallery.filename: Artillery Battalion- 1st Battle of Manassas.jpg
gallery.title: File:Artillery Battalion- 1st Battle of Manassas.jpg
gallery.description: The First Battle of Bull Run (the name used by Union forces), also known as the First Battle of Manassas[1] (the name used by Confederate forces), was the first major battle of the American Civil War and was a Confederate victory. The battle was fought on July 21, 1861 in Prince William County, Virginia, just north of the city of Manassas and about 30 miles west-southwest of Washington, D.C. The Union's forces were slow in positioning themselves, allowing Confederate reinforcements time to arrive by rail. Each side had about 18,000 poorly trained and poorly led troops in their first battle. It was a Confederate victory, followed by a disorganized retreat of the Union forces.
